bio.topic: Review: cells, movement into and out of cells, biological molecules and enzymes

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Which structure is found in plant cells but not in animal cells?
questions.hint: Think about what gives a plant cell its fixed shape.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Which is the correct formula for magnification?
questions.hint: Remember I = A × M and rearrange it.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: A drawing of a cell is 30 mm long. The magnification is ×1500. Calculate the actual length of the cell in micrometres (µm).
questions.hint: Convert mm to µm first (1 mm = 1000 µm), then divide by the magnification.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: An image of a cell is 25 mm wide. The actual width of the cell is 50 µm. Calculate the magnification of the image.
questions.hint: Make sure both measurements are in the same unit before dividing.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Which statement best defines diffusion?
options: The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, as a result of their random movement
The movement of particles against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration
The movement of water only, through a partially permeable membrane
The movement of particles from a region of lower concentration to a region of higher concentration
questions.answer: The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, as a result of their random movement
questions.hint: Diffusion is passive and goes down the concentration gradient.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Name the process by which water molecules move across a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution.
questions.hint: It is a special case of diffusion involving water.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: How is active transport different from diffusion?
options: It moves substances against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration
It only happens in dead cells
questions.answer: It moves substances against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration
questions.hint: Think about direction and energy.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: A plant cell is placed in a concentrated sugar solution. What happens to the cell?
options: It loses water by osmosis and becomes plasmolysed
It gains water by osmosis and bursts
It gains water and becomes turgid
Nothing happens because of the cell wall
questions.answer: It loses water by osmosis and becomes plasmolysed
questions.hint: Compare the water concentration inside and outside the cell.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: A potato cylinder had a mass of 2.50 g. After 30 minutes in a salt solution its mass was 2.20 g. Calculate the percentage change in mass. Give a negative sign for a loss.
questions.hint: Percentage change = (change in mass ÷ starting mass) × 100.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Which reagent is used to test for reducing sugars?
questions.hint: This test requires heating in a water bath.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: What colour does iodine solution turn when starch is present?
questions.hint: Iodine solution starts orange-brown.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: What colour indicates a positive result for protein in the biuret test?
questions.hint: The biuret reagent starts blue.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Which elements are present in all carbohydrates?
questions.hint: Proteins contain an extra element that carbohydrates do not.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: State the name of the molecule that binds to the active site of an enzyme.
questions.hint: It is the molecule that the enzyme acts on.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Explain why the activity of an enzyme decreases above its optimum temperature.
options: The shape of the active site changes so the substrate no longer fits; the enzyme is denatured
The enzyme is killed because it is a living organism
The enzyme turns into a carbohydrate
questions.answer: The shape of the active site changes so the substrate no longer fits; the enzyme is denatured
questions.hint: Enzymes are proteins; think about what heat does to their shape.

questions.subject: bio
questions.q: Explain how increasing the temperature from 20 °C to 37 °C affects the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction in the human body.
questions.hint: Use the ideas of kinetic energy, collisions and enzyme–substrate complexes.

bss.topic: Revisão do 1º term: da Proclamação da República à ditadura

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Em que ano foi proclamada a República no Brasil?
questions.hint: Foi no ano seguinte ao da abolição da escravidão.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual lema positivista foi colocado na bandeira republicana?
questions.hint: O positivismo valorizava a ordem social e o avanço científico.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Como ficou conhecido o acordo em que as elites de São Paulo e Minas Gerais se alternavam na Presidência durante a Primeira República?
questions.hint: Pense nos principais produtos de cada estado.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Como se chamava o voto controlado pelos coronéis, em que o eleitor votava no candidato indicado pelo chefe local?
questions.hint: O nome vem de um objeto usado para conduzir cavalos.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Segundo a Constituição de 1891, como era o voto no Brasil?
options: Secreto e aberto a todos os adultos
Aberto e restrito a homens alfabetizados maiores de 21 anos
Secreto e obrigatório para homens e mulheres
questions.answer: Aberto e restrito a homens alfabetizados maiores de 21 anos
questions.hint: Lembre quem ficava de fora: mulheres e analfabetos.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual revolta, ocorrida no Rio de Janeiro em 1904, foi uma reação à vacinação obrigatória e às reformas urbanas?
questions.hint: O nome da revolta lembra a campanha de saúde.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Contra o que lutaram os marinheiros na Revolta da Chibata, em 1910?
options: A cobrança de impostos sobre o café
questions.hint: A chibata era um chicote.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Que movimento armado encerrou a Primeira República em 1930?
questions.hint: O nome traz o próprio ano.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Em que ano o Código Eleitoral garantiu o direito de voto às mulheres no Brasil?
questions.hint: Foi dois anos depois do fim da Primeira República.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual destas características marcou o Estado Novo, de 1937 a 1945?
options: Eleições diretas e liberdade de imprensa
Fechamento do Congresso, censura e governo centralizado
Divisão do poder entre os coronéis
questions.answer: Fechamento do Congresso, censura e governo centralizado
questions.hint: Pense em um regime autoritário.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Que sigla designa o conjunto de leis trabalhistas reunido em 1943, que inclui carteira de trabalho e férias?
questions.hint: São três letras: Consolidação, Leis e Trabalho.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual característica marcou o período democrático de 1946 a 1964?
options: Partido único e ausência de eleições
Eleições diretas para presidente e vários partidos
Governo exercido por uma junta de militares
questions.answer: Eleições diretas para presidente e vários partidos
questions.hint: A Constituição de 1946 restaurou direitos democráticos.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Qual empresa estatal foi criada em 1953, após a campanha "O petróleo é nosso"?
questions.hint: O nome da empresa vem do recurso natural da campanha.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Uma fonte de 1968 diz: "Fica suspensa a garantia de habeas corpus nos casos de crimes políticos". A qual medida da ditadura esse trecho se refere?
questions.hint: Foi o mais duro dos atos institucionais.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Um cartaz de 1984 diz: "Eu quero votar para presidente". A que movimento ele está ligado?
questions.hint: Na época, o presidente era escolhido de forma indireta.

questions.subject: bss
questions.q: Explique por que a censura à imprensa foi importante para a manutenção da ditadura militar (1964–1985).
questions.hint: Pense no que acontece quando a população não recebe informações sobre o governo.

bus.topic: Review: understanding business activity and motivation

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which sector of the economy includes farming, fishing and mining?
questions.hint: This sector extracts natural resources.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: State the sector of the economy that a hotel belongs to.
questions.hint: Hotels provide services.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: What type of business is owned and controlled by one person who has unlimited liability?
questions.hint: Think of the simplest form of business ownership.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which feature applies to a private limited company?
options: Shares can be sold to the general public on the stock exchange
It is owned by the government
questions.hint: Think about what 'limited' in the name refers to.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which of these is an internal stakeholder?
questions.hint: Internal stakeholders work within the business.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which objective is most likely for a social enterprise?
options: Achieve social or environmental aims as well as make a profit
Increase the owner's personal wealth only
questions.answer: Achieve social or environmental aims as well as make a profit
questions.hint: The word 'social' is a clue.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which pair of stakeholder objectives is most likely to conflict?
options: Shareholders want higher dividends; employees want higher wages
Customers want quality; managers want quality
Government wants taxes paid; owners want to follow the law
Suppliers want to be paid; owners want good suppliers
questions.answer: Shareholders want higher dividends; employees want higher wages
questions.hint: Both groups want a share of the same profit.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A business has revenue of $50,000 and total costs of $38,000. Calculate its profit in dollars.
questions.hint: Profit = revenue − total costs.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A café sells 400 sandwiches at $12.50 each. Calculate its revenue in dollars.
questions.hint: Revenue = price × quantity.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A firm's sales rose from $200,000 to $250,000. Calculate the percentage increase.
questions.hint: Divide the change by the original value, then multiply by 100.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: In the hierarchy of needs, which level must be satisfied first?
questions.hint: Think about food, water and shelter.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A factory worker is paid $2 for every item produced. Which payment method is this?
questions.hint: Pay depends on the number of pieces made.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Which is a non-financial method of motivation?
questions.hint: It does not involve giving the worker money.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: In a franchise, what does the franchisee usually pay to the franchisor?
options: A fee and a royalty on sales
questions.answer: A fee and a royalty on sales
questions.hint: The franchisee pays to use the brand.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for a sole trader of changing into a private limited company.
questions.hint: Think about liability, raising finance and sharing control.

questions.subject: bus
questions.q: A bakery has high staff turnover. Analyse how job enrichment could improve the motivation of its employees.
questions.hint: Think about responsibility, interesting work and how staff might feel.

chem.topic: Review: particles, atomic structure, bonding and stoichiometry

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: What is an isotope?
options: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
Atoms of different elements with the same mass
questions.answer: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
questions.hint: Isotopes have the same number of protons.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: An atom of chlorine has atomic number 17 and mass number 35. How many neutrons does it have?
questions.hint: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Write the electronic configuration of sodium (atomic number 11).
questions.hint: Fill the shells with 2, then 8, then the rest.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: How is an ionic bond formed?
options: By transferring electrons from a metal to a non-metal
By a sea of delocalised electrons
questions.answer: By transferring electrons from a metal to a non-metal
questions.hint: Ions form when atoms gain or lose electrons.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: What is a covalent bond?
options: A shared pair of electrons between two atoms
The attraction between oppositely charged ions
The attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons
questions.answer: A shared pair of electrons between two atoms
questions.hint: Covalent bonds usually form between non-metal atoms.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Write the formula of aluminium oxide.
questions.hint: Aluminium forms 3+ ions and oxide ions are 2−.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Why does sodium chloride have a high melting point?
options: It has strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a giant lattice
It is made of small molecules
questions.answer: It has strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a giant lattice
questions.hint: Think about the type of structure in an ionic compound.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Why does graphite conduct electricity?
options: Each carbon atom has one delocalised electron that can move
It has a giant ionic lattice
Its layers are held by strong covalent bonds
questions.answer: Each carbon atom has one delocalised electron that can move
questions.hint: Each carbon forms only three covalent bonds.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Why do simple molecular substances such as water have low boiling points?
questions.hint: Boiling separates molecules, not atoms inside them.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Ammonia (Mr 17) and hydrogen chloride (Mr 36.5) are released at opposite ends of a tube. Which gas diffuses faster?
questions.hint: Compare the relative molecular masses.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of carbon dioxide, CO2. (Ar: C = 12, O = 16)
questions.hint: Add the mass of one carbon and two oxygens.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Calculate the number of moles in 9.0 g of water (Mr = 18).
questions.hint: Moles = mass ÷ Mr.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Calculate the mass, in grams, of 0.25 mol of calcium carbonate, CaCO3 (Mr = 100).
questions.hint: Mass = moles × Mr.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO. Calculate the mass, in grams, of magnesium oxide formed from 6.0 g of magnesium. (Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16)
questions.hint: Find the moles of Mg first, then use the mole ratio.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Calculate the concentration, in mol/dm³, of a solution containing 0.2 mol of solute in 500 cm³ of solution.
questions.hint: Convert cm³ to dm³ first.

questions.subject: chem
questions.q: Explain, in terms of structure and bonding, why diamond is very hard.
questions.hint: Think about how many bonds each carbon atom forms and the type of structure.

comp.topic: Term 1 review: data representation, transmission and algorithm design

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Convert the denary number 45 to an 8-bit binary number.
questions.hint: Start with the largest place value that fits into 45.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Convert the hexadecimal number 3F to denary.
questions.hint: Each hex digit is worth 16 times the digit to its right.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: An image is 800 × 600 pixels with a colour depth of 24 bits. Calculate its file size in bytes.
questions.hint: File size = width × height × colour depth, then divide by 8.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: A mono sound file is sampled at 44 100 Hz with a sample resolution of 16 bits for 10 seconds. Calculate its file size in bytes.
questions.hint: Multiply sample rate × resolution × time, then divide by 8.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which statement describes serial data transmission?
options: Several bits are sent at the same time on several wires
Data is sent one bit at a time over a single wire
Data can only travel in one direction
questions.answer: Data is sent one bit at a time over a single wire
questions.hint: Think of cars in a single lane.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which transmission mode allows data to travel in both directions, but only one direction at a time?
questions.hint: A walkie-talkie works this way.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: The 7-bit data 1011001 is sent using even parity. What parity bit (0 or 1) must be added?
questions.hint: Count the 1s already in the data.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which error detection method uses acknowledgements and timeouts to request that data is re-sent?
questions.hint: The sender waits for a reply from the receiver.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: What is a feature of symmetric encryption?
options: The same key is used to encrypt and decrypt
The public key decrypts the data
questions.answer: The same key is used to encrypt and decrypt
questions.hint: 'Symmetric' means both sides are the same.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which type of compression permanently removes some data from a file?
questions.hint: The name suggests something is lost.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q:
total ← 0
FOR i ← 1 TO 4
  total ← total + i * 2
NEXT i
OUTPUT total
What value is output?
questions.hint: Trace the loop, writing down total after each pass.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Which validation check makes sure that an exam mark is between 0 and 100?
questions.hint: The check looks at the lowest and highest allowed values.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: How does a linear search find an item in a list?
options: It checks each item in turn from the start
It always checks the middle item first
It sorts the list before searching
It only checks the last item
questions.answer: It checks each item in turn from the start
questions.hint: 'Linear' means in a line.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Explain two reasons why programmers often use hexadecimal instead of binary.
questions.hint: Think about how long binary numbers are and how easy they are to read.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Convert the 7-bit binary number 1011011 to denary.
questions.hint: Add the place values 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 where there is a 1.

questions.subject: comp
questions.q: Convert the 7-bit binary number 1101011 to hexadecimal.
questions.hint: Add a leading 0 to make 8 bits, then split into two groups of 4.

econ.topic: Term 1 review: the basic economic problem and allocation of resources

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: What is the basic economic problem?
options: Too much money in the economy
Too many firms in a market
questions.hint: Think about why choices must be made at all.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: What term describes the next best alternative given up when a choice is made?
questions.hint: It is a 'cost' that is not measured in money.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Which of these is an example of the factor of production 'capital'?
questions.hint: Capital is a man-made good used to produce other goods.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: A fall in the price of a good leads to which change on its demand curve?
options: An extension (movement down along the curve)
A shift of the curve to the right
A shift of the curve to the left
A contraction (movement up along the curve)
questions.answer: An extension (movement down along the curve)
questions.hint: A change in the good's own price causes a movement, not a shift.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Which of these would shift the demand curve for electric cars to the right?
options: A rise in the price of petrol
A rise in the price of electric cars
A new tax on electric cars
questions.answer: A rise in the price of petrol
questions.hint: Petrol cars are a substitute for electric cars.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Which of these would shift the supply curve of wheat to the left?
questions.hint: Ask which event makes it harder or more costly to produce wheat.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: If demand rises and supply stays the same, what happens to the equilibrium price and quantity?
questions.hint: Sketch the demand curve shifting right on a diagram.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: What is created in a market when the price is set above the equilibrium price: a surplus or a shortage?
questions.hint: Compare quantity supplied with quantity demanded at the higher price.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: The price of a good rises by 10% and the quantity demanded falls by 20%. Calculate the price elasticity of demand (give the value as a positive number).
questions.hint: PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: A PED value of 0.4 means demand is:
questions.hint: Compare the value with 1.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: If demand for a product is price inelastic, what happens to total revenue when the firm raises its price?
questions.hint: Quantity falls by a smaller percentage than the price rises.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Which of these is most likely to make demand for a product price elastic?
options: It takes a tiny share of income
questions.hint: Think about how easily buyers can switch.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: What is market failure?
options: When a firm makes a loss
When a shop runs out of stock for a day
questions.hint: It is about the whole allocation of resources, not one firm.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Which of these is the best example of a negative externality?
options: Noise and pollution from a factory affecting local residents
A firm paying its workers wages
A consumer buying a new phone
questions.answer: Noise and pollution from a factory affecting local residents
questions.hint: An externality affects a third party outside the transaction.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Explain why a maximum price set below equilibrium may lead to a shortage. Use the terms demand and supply.
questions.hint: Compare quantity demanded and quantity supplied at the lower price.

questions.subject: econ
questions.q: Discuss whether a government should tax sugary drinks to reduce their consumption. Consider price elasticity of demand in your answer.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to consumption if demand is inelastic, and who pays the tax.

en.topic: Term 1 review: reading skills and descriptive and narrative writing

questions.subject: en
questions.q: In a comprehension question, what does the command word 'identify' ask you to do?
options: Pick out a relevant word, phrase or fact
questions.answer: Pick out a relevant word, phrase or fact
questions.hint: It is usually a short, precise answer.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: A question asks you to answer 'in your own words'. What should you do?
options: Explain the idea without copying the text's key words
questions.answer: Explain the idea without copying the text's key words
questions.hint: The examiner wants to see that you understood the meaning.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What language technique is used here: 'The wind whispered through the trees'?
questions.hint: A non-human thing is given a human action.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which technique is used in 'Her voice was a knife cutting through the silence'?
questions.hint: Look for 'like' or 'as'. Are they there?

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What is the main effect of the short sentence in: 'The corridor stretched into darkness, every door shut tight, every light long dead. Then — a footstep.'?
questions.hint: Notice the contrast with the long sentence before it.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: When analysing a writer's effects, which answer is strongest?
options: Quote a word, explain its connotations and the effect on the reader
questions.answer: Quote a word, explain its connotations and the effect on the reader
questions.hint: Examiners reward explaining 'how' and 'why', not only 'what'.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What word describes the ideas and feelings a word suggests beyond its literal meaning?
questions.hint: 'Home' and 'house' may mean the same thing but feel different.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which sentence uses sensory imagery most effectively for descriptive writing?
options: The bitter smell of burnt toast clung to the cold kitchen walls.
There was a kitchen in the house.
I went into the kitchen and then left.
questions.answer: The bitter smell of burnt toast clung to the cold kitchen walls.
questions.hint: Look for the sentence that uses the senses.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What is the main purpose of descriptive writing?
options: To create a vivid picture of a place, person or moment
To persuade the reader to act
To tell a story with a clear plot
questions.answer: To create a vivid picture of a place, person or moment
questions.hint: Think about atmosphere rather than events.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What does a narrative need that a purely descriptive piece does not?
options: A plot with development and resolution
questions.answer: A plot with development and resolution
questions.hint: Narrative is about events that move forward.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What do we call the person or voice telling a story?
questions.hint: In 'I opened the door', this voice is first person.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Which opening hooks the reader most effectively?
options: I had exactly four minutes to decide whether to open the box.
This story is about a box.
Once upon a time there was a girl.
I woke up and had breakfast.
questions.answer: I had exactly four minutes to decide whether to open the box.
questions.hint: Which one creates a question in the reader's mind?

questions.subject: en
questions.q: What does 'show, don't tell' mean in narrative writing?
options: Reveal feelings through actions and details
questions.answer: Reveal feelings through actions and details
questions.hint: Compare 'She was nervous' with 'She twisted her ring round and round'.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: When redrafting a piece of writing, which change most improves it?
options: Replacing vague words with precise vocabulary
Making every sentence the same length
questions.answer: Replacing vague words with precise vocabulary
questions.hint: Think about accuracy and variety.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Rewrite this sentence to make it more descriptive, using at least two techniques: 'The market was busy.'
questions.hint: Try adding sensory details, a simile or a strong verb.

questions.subject: en
questions.q: Explain how a writer could use the weather to create atmosphere at the start of a narrative. Give an example sentence.
questions.hint: Think about pathetic fallacy and the mood it suggests.

en_lit.topic: Term 1 review: poetry and short stories

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What is a stanza?
options: A group of lines in a poem
The final line of a poem
A rhyme at the end of a line
questions.answer: A group of lines in a poem
questions.hint: It is like a paragraph in poetry.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What is the term for the repetition of the same consonant sound at the start of nearby words, as in 'silent, silver sea'?
questions.hint: Listen to the first sounds.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What is enjambment?
options: When a sentence runs on from one line of poetry to the next
When every line ends with a full stop
When a poem has no title
questions.answer: When a sentence runs on from one line of poetry to the next
questions.hint: Look at how the line ending interacts with the punctuation.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What is a caesura?
options: A pause in the middle of a line of poetry
A long poem that tells a story
questions.answer: A pause in the middle of a line of poetry
questions.hint: It is often marked by punctuation.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What is the term for the voice speaking in a poem, which is not always the poet?
questions.hint: We avoid saying 'the poet says' for this reason.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: A poem written in the voice of a character speaking to a silent listener is called a:
questions.hint: Think of a speech from a play, but in poem form.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: How many lines does a traditional sonnet have?
questions.hint: Shakespearean sonnets end with a rhyming couplet.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: In a short story, what is the climax?
questions.hint: It usually comes just before the resolution.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What is 'foreshadowing' in a short story?
options: Hints about what will happen later
questions.answer: Hints about what will happen later
questions.hint: Think of a warning sign early in the story.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What do we call the central idea or message a text explores, such as loss or identity?
questions.hint: It is bigger than the plot.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: What is the effect of a story ending with an unresolved or 'open' ending?
options: It leaves the reader thinking about what might happen
questions.answer: It leaves the reader thinking about what might happen
questions.hint: Consider what the reader is left with.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: Which is the best topic sentence for a literature essay paragraph?
options: The writer presents the mother as protective through the image of a closed door.
In this story there is a mother.
I liked the mother in the story.
The story was written a long time ago.
questions.answer: The writer presents the mother as protective through the image of a closed door.
questions.hint: A strong topic sentence makes a point linked to the writer's methods.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: In an essay, how should you use quotations?
options: Short, embedded quotations followed by analysis
Only quotations from the first page
questions.answer: Short, embedded quotations followed by analysis
questions.hint: Quotations support your point; they don't replace it.

questions.subject: en_lit
questions.q: In a timed essay of about 45 minutes, what is the most sensible first step?
options: Spend a few minutes planning your argument
Start writing immediately without reading the question
questions.answer: Spend a few minutes planning your argument

books.title: O Caderno Amarelo
books.premise: No último mês do primeiro período, Bento, Lia e Joana, do Clube de Leitura da biblioteca, escrevem e analisam crônicas, contos e poemas, revisando narrador, estrutura da narrativa e figuras de linguagem até o simulado com um texto inédito.

chapters.title: Capítulo 1: A fila da padaria
chapters.synopsis: Desafiado a escrever um texto próprio para o Clube de Leitura, Bento transforma a fila da padaria do bairro numa crônica e aprende o que faz esse gênero ser o que é.
chapters.text:
Bento tinha quinze anos e uma mania que os amigos achavam engraçada: anotava num caderno pequeno, de capa amarela, frases que ouvia na rua. Uma conversa no ponto de ônibus, um grito de vendedor, uma bronca de mãe no supermercado. A turma chamava aquilo de “caderno de guardados”.
Na última quarta-feira antes das provas do primeiro período, a professora Rosana, que coordenava o Clube de Leitura na biblioteca, fechou o livro que estava lendo e lançou um desafio.
— Semana que vem, cada um traz um texto seu. Pode ser conto, crônica ou poema. Depois a gente analisa tudo como se fosse um texto inédito de prova. Vale para revisar e vale para perder o medo.
Lia, a melhor amiga de Bento, já sabia que ia escrever um conto. Joana, mais tímida, disse baixinho que talvez tentasse um poema. Bento não tinha ideia nenhuma.
A ideia apareceu no dia seguinte, às sete da manhã, na fila da padaria da esquina. Bento abriu o caderno e começou a observar. Na frente dele, um senhor de chinelo contava a mesma piada que contava todos os dias, e a moça do caixa ria como se fosse a primeira vez. Um menino de uniforme contava moedas, uma por uma, para levar dois pães. Uma mulher falava ao telefone sobre o preço do tomate, e todo mundo, sem querer, opinava sobre o tomate também.
Bento voltou para casa e escreveu de uma vez só. Chamou o texto de “A fila que conversa”. Começava assim: “Na padaria da minha rua, ninguém compra só pão. Compra também dois minutos de conversa, uma piada repetida e a notícia de que o tomate subiu de novo”. E terminava com uma frase de que ele gostou muito: “Toda fila é uma pequena cidade, com seus moradores, suas leis e seus palhaços”.
Na quarta seguinte, ele leu o texto em voz alta. Ficou vermelho no começo, mas a turma riu nos lugares certos.
— É crônica — disse Lia, assim que ele terminou. — Você partiu de um fato do dia a dia e chegou numa reflexão.
— E a linguagem é parecida com a fala — completou Joana. — Parece que você está conversando com a gente.
A professora Rosana concordou e escreveu no quadro as marcas que eles tinham encontrado: assunto do cotidiano, texto curto, narrador que observa e comenta, tom leve, às vezes bem-humorado, e uma reflexão no final.
— Muitas crônicas nasceram nos jornais — explicou ela. — O nome vem de uma palavra grega ligada ao tempo. O cronista olha para o próprio tempo e para o que quase ninguém repara.
— Então eu sou cronista? — perguntou Bento, desconfiado.
— Hoje você foi — respondeu a professora, sorrindo.
Naquela noite, Bento abriu o caderno amarelo e escreveu na primeira página, com letra caprichada: “Guardar frases também é um jeito de escrever”. Depois ficou pensando no que Lia traria na semana seguinte.

chapters.title: Capítulo 2: Quem conta o conto
chapters.synopsis: Lia apresenta um conto de suspense narrado em primeira pessoa, e o clube descobre o que muda quando se troca o narrador de uma história.
chapters.text:
Lia chegou à biblioteca com três folhas grampeadas e um sorriso de quem guardava um segredo. O conto dela se chamava “A chave do 302”.
A história era narrada por uma menina de doze anos. Num sábado de chuva, ela encontrava uma chave antiga, presa a um chaveiro de madeira com o número 302, caída na escada do prédio. Ninguém no prédio dizia ser o dono. A menina passava a semana investigando: perguntava ao porteiro, deixava bilhetes no elevador, desconfiava da vizinha do quinto andar. No final, descobria que a chave era da própria avó, que tinha morado no apartamento 302 quando era jovem e guardava aquela lembrança no bolso do casaco havia cinquenta anos.
Quando Lia terminou de ler, Joana bateu palmas devagar.
— Eu não esperava que fosse a avó!
A professora Rosana pediu que eles identificassem os elementos da narrativa. Bento foi ao quadro: personagens, a menina, a avó, o porteiro e a vizinha; espaço, o prédio, sobretudo a escada e o elevador; tempo, uma semana de chuva; conflito, descobrir de quem era a chave.
— E quem conta a história? — perguntou a professora.
— A própria menina — respondeu Lia. — Narradora-personagem, em primeira pessoa.
— Então vamos fazer uma experiência. Reescreva o primeiro parágrafo em terceira pessoa, com um narrador que sabe tudo, até o que as personagens pensam.
Lia pegou o lápis e, depois de alguns minutos, leu: “A menina encontrou a chave na escada. Não sabia que, três andares acima, a avó procurava aquela mesma chave no bolso do casaco, com o coração apertado”.
Houve um silêncio na mesa.
— Estragou a surpresa — disse Bento. — Agora o leitor já sabe que é da avó.
— Exatamente — disse a professora. — O narrador onisciente sabe o que todos sentem e pensam. A narradora-personagem só sabe o que vê, ouve e imagina. Por isso, no conto da Lia, o leitor descobre as coisas junto com ela.
Joana levantou a mão, meio sem jeito.
— Mas o narrador em terceira pessoa também poderia esconder a informação, não poderia?
— Poderia, se fosse um narrador observador, que conta só o que se vê de fora. Toda escolha de narrador é uma escolha sobre o que o leitor vai saber e quando.
Lia passou o resto da tarde riscando e reescrevendo. Experimentou o narrador observador, depois voltou para a primeira pessoa. No fim, manteve a versão original, mas acrescentou uma frase no último parágrafo: “Naquele dia eu entendi que algumas chaves não abrem portas, abrem lembranças”.
— Agora sim — ela disse, satisfeita. — Antes eu escolhi a primeira pessoa sem pensar. Agora eu sei por quê.
Na saída, Bento anotou no caderno amarelo: “O narrador é o dono das portas: decide quais o leitor pode abrir”. Joana, ao lado dele, apertava contra o peito uma folha dobrada em quatro. Era o poema dela, e ela ainda não tinha coragem de mostrar.

chapters.title: Capítulo 3: O poema sem rima
chapters.synopsis: Joana finalmente lê seu poema sobre um varal, com medo de que não seja poesia por não rimar, e o clube descobre o verso livre, o eu lírico e as figuras de linguagem.
chapters.text:
Joana demorou para desdobrar a folha. Quando finalmente o fez, avisou antes de começar:
— Não rima. Acho que não é um poema de verdade.
— Lê primeiro — pediu a professora Rosana. — Depois a gente decide.
Joana respirou fundo e leu:
“Minha mãe estende as camisas / como quem escreve uma frase: / uma palavra azul, outra branca, / e um ponto final de meia. // O vento chega sem pedir licença / e lê tudo em voz alta, / balançando as mangas / como braços que se despedem. // À tarde, recolho a frase inteira, / seca, dobrada, quieta. / Ninguém percebe, / mas a casa ficou com cheiro de sol.”
Ninguém disse nada por alguns segundos. Depois Lia falou:
— Joana, isso é lindo.
A professora copiou o poema no quadro, verso por verso, e começou as perguntas.
— Quantas estrofes?
— Três — respondeu Bento.
— E quantos versos em cada uma?
— Quatro. Doze versos no total.
— Muito bem. Agora, a rima. Joana tem razão: não há rimas regulares. Isso tem nome: verso livre. Muitos poetas escrevem assim. O que faz um texto ser poema não é só a rima, é o trabalho com o ritmo, com as imagens e com o som das palavras.
Joana ergueu os olhos pela primeira vez desde o início da leitura.
Em seguida, a professora pediu que procurassem as figuras de linguagem. Lia encontrou a primeira: “como quem escreve uma frase” era uma comparação, porque aproximava duas coisas usando a palavra “como”. Bento achou a segunda: o vento que “lê tudo em voz alta” era uma personificação, já que dava ao vento uma ação humana.
— E a frase de roupas? — perguntou a professora. — As camisas viram palavras, a meia vira ponto final. Não há “como” aqui.
— Metáfora — disse Joana, surpresa com a própria voz.
— E “cheiro de sol”? Sol tem cheiro?
— Não — riu Bento. — Mistura o olfato com uma coisa que a gente vê e sente na pele.
— Isso se chama sinestesia: a mistura de sentidos.
Por último, a professora falou de algo que deixou Joana pensativa.
— Quem fala no poema é o eu lírico. Pode ser parecido com a autora, mas não é a mesma pessoa. O eu lírico é uma voz criada dentro do texto.
— Então eu posso escrever sobre um varal que não é o da minha casa?
— Pode. E pode escrever sobre o da sua casa sem que o poema seja um diário.
No fim do encontro, a professora perguntou se Joana deixaria o poema no mural da biblioteca. Ela hesitou, olhou para Lia, olhou para Bento e disse que sim.
Na saída, ela parou diante do mural e leu o próprio texto de novo, agora em letra de quadro, como se fosse de outra pessoa. Gostou. Bento, discreto, anotou no caderno amarelo: “Rima é só uma das músicas possíveis”.

chapters.title: Capítulo 4: O guarda-chuva esquecido
chapters.synopsis: A professora traz um conto inédito para o clube analisar como numa prova, e Bento e Joana discordam sobre qual é o clímax da história.
chapters.text:
Na quarta seguinte, a professora Rosana entregou a cada um uma folha com um conto curto, sem nome de autor.
— Texto inédito — anunciou. — Ninguém aqui leu antes. É assim que vai ser na prova.
O conto se chamava “O guarda-chuva”. Contava a história de Teodoro, um senhor de cabelos brancos que esperava o ônibus todas as manhãs no mesmo ponto, sempre com um guarda-chuva preto, fizesse sol ou chuva. E todas as manhãs ele o esquecia no banco. Clara, uma menina que esperava o ônibus da escola ali perto, corria atrás dele e devolvia o guarda-chuva. Ele agradecia com o mesmo aceno de chapéu. Isso durou um ano inteiro. Um dia, Teodoro não apareceu. Nem no dia seguinte, nem na semana seguinte. O guarda-chuva ficou no banco. Clara o levou para casa e passou a carregá-lo para a escola. Numa tarde de tempestade, ela o abriu pela primeira vez e um papel caiu do meio das varetas: “Obrigado por correr atrás de mim todos os dias. Era a melhor parte da minha manhã”.
A professora pediu que eles dividissem o conto nas partes da narrativa.
Lia começou pela situação inicial: a rotina de Teodoro e Clara no ponto de ônibus. Depois veio a complicação: o dia em que Teodoro não aparece.
Foi aí que a discussão começou.
— O clímax é quando ele some — disse Bento. — É a hora de mais tensão. A gente fica preocupado.
— Não é — discordou Joana, com uma firmeza que surpreendeu todo mundo. — O clímax é quando o bilhete cai. É ali que tudo muda de sentido. A gente descobre que o esquecimento talvez fosse de propósito.
— Os dois estão defendendo uma ideia — disse a professora. — Numa prova, as duas leituras poderiam ganhar pontos, desde que vocês justifiquem com o texto. Qual trecho comprova o que dizem?
Joana leu em voz alta a frase do bilhete. Explicou que, antes dele, a história parecia ser sobre um senhor distraído. Depois dele, passava a ser sobre amizade e solidão. O ponto de virada estava ali.
Bento pensou um pouco e concordou em parte.
— Tá. O sumiço cria a tensão, mas o bilhete é o momento mais forte. Talvez o sumiço seja a complicação e o bilhete seja o clímax.
— E o desfecho? — perguntou a professora.
Ninguém soube responder de primeira. O conto terminava com o bilhete. Não dizia o que tinha acontecido com Teodoro.
— É um final aberto — disse Lia. — O leitor tem que imaginar.
— Exatamente. E um final aberto não é um defeito. É uma escolha do autor. Ele confia no leitor.
Na volta para casa, Bento começou a reparar nas pessoas do ponto de ônibus. Um rapaz com fone de ouvido, uma senhora com sacolas, uma criança dormindo no colo do pai. Pensou que cada um deles poderia ser o começo de um conto. Abriu o caderno amarelo e escreveu: “Clímax é o momento em que a história vira do avesso”.

chapters.title: Capítulo 5: Crônica ou conto?
chapters.synopsis: Um texto do jornal do bairro sobre um pombo que entrou no metrô divide o clube: é crônica ou conto? A turma descobre que as fronteiras entre os gêneros podem ser finas.
chapters.text:
Lia chegou agitada, com um recorte de jornal na mão.
— Achei no jornalzinho do bairro. É de uma colunista que escreve toda semana. Mas eu não sei se é crônica ou conto.
O texto se chamava “O passageiro de penas”. A colunista contava que, numa segunda-feira de manhã, um pombo tinha entrado no vagão do metrô em que ela estava. O pombo andava entre os pés das pessoas com uma calma de executivo atrasado. Uma senhora disse que ele ia descer na estação da Sé. Um rapaz apostou que ia para a Paulista. Durante três estações, desconhecidos que nunca se olhavam conversaram, riram e torceram pelo pombo. Quando as portas se abriram, ele desceu, sem pressa, na estação errada para todos os palpites. O texto terminava assim: “Precisamos de um pombo por semana para lembrar que estamos no mesmo vagão”.
— É crônica — disse Bento logo. — Saiu no jornal, é do dia a dia, termina com uma reflexão. Igual à minha da padaria.
— Mas tem personagens, tempo, espaço, conflito… — rebateu Lia. — Tem até uma pequena tensão: onde o pombo vai descer? Parece conto.
Joana, que agora falava muito mais nos encontros, levantou outra questão.
— E aconteceu de verdade? Porque, se for inventado, é conto, não é?
A professora Rosana sorriu, como se estivesse esperando exatamente aquela pergunta.
— Vocês três têm um pouco de razão. Existem crônicas que narram uma pequena história, com personagens e acontecimentos. Muita gente chama isso de crônica narrativa. O que pesa mais é o conjunto: o texto parte do cotidiano, está ligado ao tempo presente, tem tom de conversa com o leitor e quer provocar uma reflexão sobre a vida comum.
— E se a colunista inventou o pombo? — insistiu Joana.
— O cronista pode recriar, exagerar, enfeitar. O leitor da crônica não pede um documento; pede um olhar. Já o conto costuma construir um mundo fechado, com um conflito que se desenvolve até um clímax. No pombo, o mais importante não é o mistério da estação. É o que ele faz com as pessoas.
Bento folheou o caderno amarelo e leu uma anotação antiga: “Toda fila é uma pequena cidade”.
— É a mesma coisa! — exclamou. — O vagão é a minha fila.
— Então vocês já sabem o que responder se isso cair na prova — disse a professora. — Não basta dizer o nome do gênero. É preciso apontar as marcas no texto.
Para treinar, ela propôs um jogo: cada um diria uma característica do texto e a qual gênero ela se aproximava mais. Lia ficou com as marcas do conto. Bento ficou com as da crônica. Joana, como juíza, decidia. No fim, o placar foi de cinco a três para a crônica.
— Crônica narrativa — decretou Joana, batendo a caneta na mesa como um martelo.
Todos riram. Lia guardou o recorte no meio do livro que estava lendo, como quem guarda uma folha seca. Na semana seguinte, porém, nenhum deles imaginava que a aula ia acontecer no escuro.

chapters.title: Capítulo 6: Figuras no apagão
chapters.synopsis: Uma tempestade apaga as luzes da biblioteca, e a professora transforma a escuridão num jogo em que os alunos caçam figuras de linguagem nas próprias falas.
chapters.text:
A tempestade começou no meio do encontro. Primeiro um vento forte balançou as janelas da biblioteca, depois veio a chuva grossa e, de repente, as luzes se apagaram. Ficou só a claridade cinzenta que entrava pelas janelas altas.
— Está chovendo canivete! — disse Bento.
— A biblioteca virou uma caverna — sussurrou Joana.
Um trovão longo fez as estantes vibrarem.
— O céu está resmungando — comentou Lia. — Deve estar de mau humor.
A professora Rosana acendeu a lanterna do celular e apontou para o teto, deixando a mesa numa luz amarela e fraca.
— Vocês perceberam o que acabaram de fazer? Em menos de um minuto, usaram três figuras de linguagem. Vamos aproveitar o escuro. Ninguém vai embora com essa chuva mesmo.
Ela propôs um jogo: cada um diria uma frase sobre a tempestade, e os outros teriam de descobrir a figura.
Bento começou pelo próprio exemplo.
— “Está chovendo canivete” é uma expressão popular, mas também é um exagero. Ninguém acha que caem facas do céu.
— Hipérbole — disse Lia. — O exagero de propósito para dar força.
— E “a biblioteca virou uma caverna”? — perguntou a professora.
— Metáfora — respondeu Joana. — Não tem “como”. A biblioteca simplesmente vira outra coisa.
— Se eu dissesse “a biblioteca está escura como uma caverna”?
— Aí é comparação — completou Bento. — Por causa do “como”.
Lia ficou com o céu resmungão.
— Personificação, porque o céu ganhou humor de gente.
Depois disso o jogo pegou fogo. Bento disse que já tinha avisado mil vezes que ia chover; Joana apontou outra hipérbole. Lia falou de um “silêncio barulhento” que tomou a sala entre um trovão e outro, e a professora explicou que juntar ideias opostas tinha um nome: antítese, ou, quando as duas aparecem coladas, paradoxo. Joana, inspirada, criou uma frase de propósito:
— “Chuva, chuva, chuva na chapa do telhado.”
— Repetição e aliteração! — disse Bento, rindo. — Esse som de “ch” parece a própria chuva.
A professora aplaudiu.
— Agora o mais importante. Na prova, não basta dar nome à figura. Vocês precisam explicar o efeito. Por que dizer que o céu resmunga, e não só que trovejou?
Lia pensou.
— Porque assim o trovão parece uma pessoa irritada. Fica mais vivo, e o leitor quase ouve o resmungo.
— Isso vale ponto — disse a professora.
Quando as luzes voltaram, quarenta minutos depois, todos piscaram como se tivessem acordado. Joana já tinha enchido uma página inteira com as frases do jogo, cada uma com o nome da figura ao lado. Bento copiou a lista no caderno amarelo e acrescentou no final, sublinhado duas vezes: “Nomear a figura é achar a chave. Explicar o efeito é abrir a porta”.
— Semana que vem é o simulado — lembrou a professora, apagando a lanterna. — Quarenta minutos, um texto inédito. Tragam a coragem.

chapters.title: Capítulo 7: Quarenta minutos
chapters.synopsis: No simulado, Bento enfrenta um poema inédito com o relógio correndo e usa tudo o que o clube aprendeu no período para escrever sua análise.
chapters.text:
No dia do simulado, a biblioteca estava silenciosa demais. A professora Rosana colocou um relógio grande em cima da mesa e distribuiu as folhas viradas para baixo.
— Quarenta minutos. Um poema inédito e uma pergunta. Podem virar.
O poema se chamava “Escada”. Tinha duas estrofes curtas: “Subo os degraus de dois em dois / quando a pressa me empurra. / Desço de um em um / quando a saudade me segura. // Entre o térreo e o último andar / mora a minha vida inteira: / cada degrau, um ano; / cada corrimão, alguém que me esperou.”
A pergunta dizia: “Analise como o eu lírico apresenta a passagem do tempo no poema. Use trechos do texto para justificar sua resposta”.
Bento sentiu o estômago gelar. Por um minuto inteiro, ficou olhando para a folha sem ler nada. Depois lembrou do caderno amarelo, que estava na mochila, e das frases que tinha anotado durante o período. Não podia abri-lo, mas lembrava delas.
Respirou e seguiu o método que a turma tinha montado junto. Primeiro, ler o poema duas vezes, uma para entender e outra para marcar. Segundo, perguntar quem fala e sobre o quê. Terceiro, procurar os recursos. Quarto, explicar o efeito de cada um.
Na segunda leitura, ele circulou “pressa me empurra” e “saudade me segura”. Escreveu na margem: personificação, sentimentos agindo como pessoas. Sublinhou “cada degrau, um ano”: metáfora, a escada é a vida. Notou também a oposição entre subir e descer, entre a pressa e a saudade. Lembrou da antítese da tarde do apagão.
Então começou a escrever. Explicou que o eu lírico representa a vida como uma escada, em que cada degrau corresponde a um ano. Mostrou que a pressa e a saudade aparecem como forças que empurram e seguram, o que faz o leitor sentir o tempo no próprio corpo. Disse que a oposição entre subir de dois em dois e descer de um em um mostrava duas maneiras de viver o tempo: correndo para o futuro ou voltando devagar ao passado. Terminou com o último verso: o corrimão representava as pessoas que apoiaram o eu lírico pelo caminho.
Quando a professora avisou que faltavam cinco minutos, Bento releu o texto, corrigiu duas vírgulas e colocou um ponto final que lhe pareceu definitivo.
Na quarta seguinte, as folhas voltaram corrigidas. Ao lado do parágrafo de Bento sobre a pressa e a saudade, a professora tinha escrito: “Ótimo. Você não só nomeou a figura: explicou o efeito”. Lia tinha ido bem na estrutura. Joana tinha feito a melhor análise do último verso, e a professora leu um trecho dela em voz alta. Joana não ficou vermelha. Sorriu.
Para comemorar o fim do período, a professora trouxe pão de queijo da padaria da esquina. Bento reconheceu o saquinho e riu sozinho.
— Que foi? — perguntou Lia.
— Nada. Essa padaria já virou crônica.
Antes de ir embora, ele abriu o caderno amarelo numa página nova e escreveu: “Primeiro período: aprendi que todo texto tem uma porta. E que a chave quase sempre está nos detalhes”.

books.subject: en_lit
books.title: The Lantern Hour
books.premise: In the last weeks of term, Noor, Tomás and Elsie revise poetry and short stories at the library window table, while trying to discover who is secretly pinning unsigned poems to the noticeboard.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Poem on the Noticeboard
chapters.synopsis: Noor finds an unsigned poem pinned in the library and the revision group analyses its imagery. They agree to find out who wrote it before the end of term.
chapters.text:
It was the second-to-last week of term, and the library smelled of radiators and old paper. Noor Haddad had come in early to claim the big table by the window for the revision group, but something on the noticeboard stopped her.
Between a poster about lost property and a timetable for the chess club, someone had pinned a single sheet of lined paper. There was no name on it, only a title written in careful capitals: TIDE.
"The city comes in like the sea at six, / grey water pouring down the stairs of the station, / and we are shells it carries, / rattling, turning, never choosing where we land."
Noor read it twice. Then she unpinned it, a little guiltily, and laid it on the table just as Tomás and Elsie arrived, shaking the rain from their coats.
"Is that homework?" Tomás asked.
"Better," said Noor. "It's evidence. Someone in this school writes poems and hides them."
Elsie, who never went anywhere without three colours of highlighter, was already leaning over the page. "Extended metaphor," she said. "The whole city is the sea. The commuters are the water, and then the speaker switches, and the people become shells."
"So which is it?" Tomás frowned. "Are people the sea or the shells?"
"Both," said Noor slowly. "That's the point, isn't it? First the crowd is powerful, pouring down the stairs. Then, when the poem says 'we', it gets small. Inside the crowd you're just carried along."
Elsie underlined "rattling, turning" in green. "Present participles. They keep everything moving. And 'never choosing where we land' sounds sad to me. Like the speaker feels they've got no control."
Tomás tapped the word "six". "Six in the morning or six in the evening?"
"Does it matter?" asked Elsie.
"If it's the evening, the tide is going home. If it's morning, it's going to work. Different mood."
Noor wrote both readings in the margin of her notebook. Ms Ferrant, their English teacher, always said that an unseen poem was a locked door with more than one key, and that good answers tried at least two keys before choosing one.
By the time the bell rang, the sheet was covered in the group's notes, written lightly in pencil so they could be rubbed out. Noor pinned the poem back exactly where she had found it.
"We should find out who wrote it," Tomás said as they packed up.
"Before the end of term," Elsie agreed.
Noor looked at the capital letters once more. Whoever the poet was, they had pressed hard enough to dent the paper. That, she thought, was a clue of its own.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Weekend That Didn't Happen
chapters.synopsis: Tomás tells a dramatic story about his weekend and the others spot that he is an unreliable narrator. The group links the game to narrative voice in short stories.
chapters.text:
On Tuesday, Tomás arrived at the window table looking very pleased with himself.
"You will not believe my weekend," he announced. "I rescued a dog from the canal. A huge one. I jumped in, pulled it out, and the owner was so grateful that she cried. Then I went home and finished all my revision."
Elsie put down her highlighter. "All of it?"
"All of it."
"You jumped into the canal," said Noor. "In November."
"It wasn't that cold," Tomás said, and then, a moment later, "It was a medium-sized dog."
Elsie began to smile. "A minute ago it was huge."
"It looked huge from the bridge."
"So you were on the bridge," Noor said. "Not in the water."
Tomás folded his arms, but his ears had gone pink. "Fine. I saw a man throw a stick, and the dog jumped in, and it swam out by itself. I clapped. That was the rescue."
Everyone laughed, Tomás loudest of all. Then Noor sat up straight. "Wait. That's exactly what we need for the short story question. Unreliable narrators."
She opened her anthology to a story they had studied in October, told by a boy who insisted he wasn't afraid of the dark while describing every shadow in the house. "How did we know he was unreliable?"
"He kept contradicting himself," Elsie said. "Like Tomás and the dog."
"And other characters didn't react the way he said they would," Noor added. "That's a clue too. The narrator tells us one thing, but the details tell us another."
Tomás leaned forward, interested now. "So the reader knows more than the narrator. That's dramatic irony, isn't it?"
"Sort of," said Elsie. "It's what makes it funny, or sad, depending on the story."
They spent the next half hour building a list on the back of a revision sheet: contradictions, exaggerations, gaps in time, other characters' reactions, a narrator who protests too much. Next to each, Noor wrote what effect it might have on a reader.
At the end, Elsie held up the sheet. "We should test this. Everyone brings a short story tomorrow, told by an unreliable narrator. The others have to find the clues."
"I'll bring a true one," said Tomás.
"Will you?" asked Noor.
Tomás grinned and did not answer.
As they left, Noor glanced at the noticeboard. A second sheet of lined paper had appeared beside the first. The capitals read: HONEST.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Ring in the Biscuit Tin
chapters.synopsis: Elsie tells a family story with a twist ending, and the group studies how foreshadowing and circular structure make it work. They realise the hidden poet notices small details too.
chapters.text:
Elsie's story was not about herself. It was about her grandmother.
"When Gran was nineteen," she began, "she worked in a bakery by the harbour. Every morning a fisherman bought one plain biscuit and paid with exact change. Every morning he said the same thing: 'One day I'll buy the whole tin.'"
Noor stopped writing. Tomás stopped eating his apple.
"Then one winter his boat didn't come back on time. Three days late. Gran kept a biscuit aside for him every morning, wrapped in paper, until the shelf was full of little parcels. On the fourth day he walked in, soaked, and put a whole handful of coins on the counter."
"For the whole tin," said Tomás.
"For the whole tin," Elsie agreed. "And when Gran opened it to count the biscuits, there was a ring inside, tied to the lid with fishing line. He'd been hiding it in his coat for months, waiting for the right moment."
For a second nobody spoke. Then Tomás said, "Is that true?"
"Gran says so. She still has the tin. We keep buttons in it."
Noor tapped her pencil against the table. "That's a perfect example for structure, though. Listen. The story opens with the line about the whole tin, and it ends with the whole tin. That's circular structure. The ending echoes the beginning, but it means something new."
"And it's foreshadowed," Elsie said. "The 'one day' line sounds like a joke at first. You only realise afterwards that he meant it."
Tomás frowned thoughtfully. "What about the three days? That's the tension. The writer, or Gran, slows everything down with the little parcels on the shelf. You can picture them piling up."
"Exactly," said Noor. "If you just said 'he was late and then he came back', there'd be no suspense. The parcels show time passing and show how worried she was, without saying 'she was worried'."
"Show, don't tell," said all three of them at once, in Ms Ferrant's voice, and then laughed.
They drew a diagram of the story on a fresh page: exposition at the bakery, rising tension during the storm, the climax when the tin opens, and the resolution in the present day, with buttons inside. Noor added a small arrow curving from the end back to the beginning.
On the way out, they checked the noticeboard. There was no new poem today. But someone had added two pencil words beneath HONEST, in the same pressed-hard capitals: TRY AGAIN.
"They've read our notes," said Elsie.
"Or they're writing to themselves," said Noor.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Rain on the Roof
chapters.synopsis: A power cut leaves the group reading poems aloud by torchlight, and they discover how sound devices and enjambment shape meaning. A new poem appears that seems to answer their discussion.
chapters.text:
On Thursday the storm arrived properly. Halfway through the revision session, the lights in the library flickered twice and went out.
The librarian's voice came from somewhere near the returns desk. "Stay where you are, everyone. The caretaker's on his way."
Tomás switched on the torch on his phone and propped it against a dictionary. Rain hammered on the flat roof above them, a steady, hissing roar.
"Well," said Noor, "we can't highlight anything. Let's read aloud instead."
She chose a poem from the anthology about a river in flood, and read it slowly. When she reached the line "sliding, slipping, swallowing the stones", Elsie held up a hand.
"Listen to that," she said. "All those s sounds. It's sibilance. It sounds like the rain right now."
"It sounds like water moving," Tomás agreed. "Smooth, but a bit sinister. Like it's whispering."
Noor read on. One sentence ran across three lines without stopping, and her voice had to carry over the line breaks to keep the sense.
"That's enjambment," Elsie said. "The sentence spills over the line ending, like the river spilling over the bank."
"So the form copies the meaning," said Noor. "That's the sort of thing examiners love. Not just naming the device, but saying why it's there."
Tomás tried the next stanza. It was different: short lines, each ending in a full stop. "Stop. Wait. Breathe. The bank holds."
"Caesura and end-stopping," said Noor. "After all that rushing, the full stops slow it down. It feels like relief."
"Or like someone holding their breath," Tomás said. "It isn't safe yet. It just says the bank holds. For now."
They were quiet for a moment, listening to the real rain. In the half-dark, the poem felt less like homework and more like something happening around them.
When the lights came back on, there was a small cheer from the other tables. The caretaker, a tall man with a toolbox and a wet cap, waved from the doorway and disappeared again.
As they packed up, Elsie noticed a third sheet on the noticeboard, pinned so recently that the drawing pin still shone. It was titled STORM, and its lines were full of hissing s sounds and long sentences that tumbled from one line into the next, until the very last line, which said simply: "Then the lights."
Noor stared at it. "That wasn't there when we came in."
"So the poet was here," said Tomás, "during the power cut."
They looked around the library. At least twenty people had been in the room.

chapters.title: Chapter 5: The Lighthouse That Wasn't
chapters.synopsis: In a revision lesson about setting, the group writes about a lighthouse and argues over what it symbolises. They notice that the hidden poet's poems all share one setting.
chapters.text:
On Friday Ms Ferrant gave the class a picture prompt for a practice short story: a lighthouse on a rocky headland, its lamp unlit, with a single gull on the rail.
"Twenty minutes," she said. "Focus on setting. Make the place do some of the work."
Noor wrote about a lighthouse keeper's daughter who climbs the tower every evening, even though the lamp has been automatic for years. Elsie wrote from the gull's point of view, which made Tomás laugh out loud and earned him a look from Ms Ferrant. Tomás wrote about a storm, because, he said, he was still thinking about the power cut.
Afterwards, in the library, they compared.
"The lighthouse is a symbol," said Elsie. "It always is. Safety. Guidance. Hope."
"But mine was unlit," Noor said. "So in my story it isn't about safety. It's about something nobody needs anymore, and the girl climbs up anyway because it used to matter. It's about memory."
Tomás chewed his pen. "Then can a symbol mean opposite things?"
"It depends on the details around it," said Noor. "A lit lighthouse in a storm means rescue. An unlit one in calm weather might mean loneliness, or being forgotten. The writer decides by choosing the setting."
Elsie added a line to their revision sheet: Setting reflects mood. Symbols change meaning with context.
"Pathetic fallacy," said Tomás, pleased to remember a term. "My storm matched the character's anger."
"Good," said Noor. "But don't just name it. Say what it does. Does the storm make the anger feel bigger? Does it warn us something bad will happen?"
"Both," said Tomás. "Obviously." He wrote it down anyway.
While they talked, Elsie had laid the three poems from the noticeboard side by side; she had copied them into her notebook each day. Suddenly she sat back.
"Look at the settings. TIDE is the station at six. HONEST mentions a corridor with the lights switched off. STORM is the library in a power cut. They're all school or nearby. And all of them happen when the building is empty or nearly empty."
"Early morning, late evening," said Noor slowly. "Times when most students aren't here."
Tomás raised his eyebrows. "So the poet is someone who's around when nobody else is."
"Or someone who notices the building when it's quiet," Elsie said. "Like a setting in a story. The place is doing the work."
Noor looked down at her own story, at the girl climbing the old tower to see a light nobody else cared about. She felt, without quite knowing why, that they were getting close.

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Forty-Five Minutes
chapters.synopsis: In the timed practice essay, Noor panics when she sees an unfamiliar poem, then uses the group's planning method to finish. The friends learn that a clear plan matters more than knowing every term.
chapters.text:
On Monday of the last week, Ms Ferrant handed out the timed essay. "Forty-five minutes," she said. "One unseen poem. How does the poet present the speaker's feelings about change? Plan first."
Noor turned the page over and her stomach dropped. The poem was about moving house, but it was strange: no rhyme, odd gaps in the middle of lines, and an ending that seemed to say nothing at all. "The boxes. The window. The boxes."
For a whole minute she simply stared. She could hear Tomás's pen already scratching beside her. Her mind felt as empty as the rooms in the poem.
Then she remembered the window table, the pencil notes, the locked door with more than one key. She made herself breathe and wrote three words at the top of the page: WHAT, HOW, WHY.
What does the speaker feel? Sad, but also something else. Numb, maybe. How does the poet show it? The gaps in the lines, like pauses, like someone who can't finish a thought. The repetition of "boxes", flat and heavy. Why? To show that big changes can leave you too stunned to describe them.
She jotted a quick plan: an opening sentence answering the question directly, three paragraphs, each with a short quotation, a technique and its effect on the reader, then a final paragraph trying a second key: perhaps the window at the end was hopeful, a view of somewhere new.
The panic shrank. It did not vanish, but it became small enough to write around.
At the end of the forty-five minutes, her hand ached. She had not used every term she knew. She had not mentioned iambic anything. But every paragraph answered the question, and her last paragraph argued that the repeated "boxes" were packed with things the speaker could not yet say.
In the library afterwards, the three of them compared notes.
"I wrote too much on the first stanza," Tomás admitted. "I ran out of time for the ending."
"I listed devices," said Elsie, "but I'm not sure I explained them."
"I nearly wrote nothing," said Noor. "Then I just started with what I felt, and worked out how the poem made me feel it."
Elsie added a final rule to their sheet, in purple: Plan for five minutes. Answer the question in your first sentence. Effect, not just device.
On the noticeboard there was a new poem. It was called EXAM, and it was about watching rows of students from the doorway, heads bent, and wishing them luck without being able to say it. The last line read: "I keep the building warm for them."
Noor read it and felt something click into place.

chapters.title: Chapter 7: The Lantern Hour
chapters.synopsis: The group discovers that the hidden poet is the school caretaker and invites him to read at the end-of-term gathering. Noor realises the term's revision has changed how she reads.
chapters.text:
On the last Wednesday of term, Noor came in earlier than ever. The library was dark except for the security lights, and the radiators were only beginning to tick. She sat at the window table and waited.
At ten to seven, the door opened. The caretaker came in with his toolbox, the same wet cap from the night of the storm, and a sheet of lined paper folded in his top pocket. He walked to the noticeboard, took out a drawing pin, and stopped when he saw her.
"Ah," he said. "Caught."
"I'm sorry," said Noor quickly. "We weren't spying. Well, a bit. We've been reading your poems all term. They helped us revise."
He laughed, and some of the stiffness went out of his shoulders. His name was Mr Okafor, he said, and he had written poems since he was a boy, in notebooks nobody ever saw. "I come in before everyone and leave after everyone. The building's a different place when it's empty. I wanted to put something back into it."
"Why no name?" Noor asked.
He thought about it. "A name makes people decide what a poem means before they read it. Without one, they just read."
When Elsie and Tomás arrived, they found Noor and Mr Okafor arguing cheerfully about whether TIDE was set in the morning or the evening. He refused to say. "That's your job," he told them. "I only wrote it."
That afternoon, at the end-of-term gathering in the hall, Ms Ferrant asked if anyone had something to share. Tomás, to everyone's surprise, stood up first and told the true story of the dog, the stick and the bridge. It got the biggest laugh of the day.
Then Elsie read her gran's story about the biscuit tin, and the hall went very quiet.
Last of all, Noor walked to the back of the room, where Mr Okafor was standing by the door with his toolbox, and asked if he would read. He hesitated for a long moment. Then he took the folded paper from his pocket.
The poem was called LANTERN HOUR. It was about the time between the last student leaving and the lights going off, when the corridors still hold the shapes of voices. It ended: "and I walk through what you leave behind, / and find it is enough to light the way."
Nobody clapped at first. They were still listening. Then everyone did.
On the bus home, Noor took out her revision sheet, crowded with pencil, highlighter and purple rules. She realised she no longer read poems as puzzles with one right answer. She read them as doors, and she had a pocket full of keys.
